definition: not certain or fixed; done without confidence

examples.text: The team reached a tentative conclusion that will need more data to confirm.
The two governments signed a tentative agreement, subject to approval at home.
We made tentative plans for Saturday, depending on the weather.

confused.note: Tentative means hesitant or provisional; tenacious means holding on firmly.

questions.passage: The authors are careful not to overstate their findings. They describe the link between the gene and the disease as ______, noting that it has so far been observed in only one small group of patients.
questions.explanation: A link seen in only one small group is provisional and uncertain.

distractors.why: Conclusive means settling the matter, which a single small study cannot do.
Flagrant means shockingly obvious wrongdoing, which does not describe a research finding.
Incessant means never stopping, which does not fit a link between gene and disease.

definition: intended to cause a strong reaction, such as anger, interest, or debate

examples.text: The essay opens with a provocative claim: that most classics are overrated.
The envoy's provocative speech nearly ended the peace talks.
She wore a provocative T-shirt that read "Your Team Is Mediocre."

confused.note: Provocative means stirring up a reaction or argument; evocative means calling up memories or feelings.

questions.passage: The exhibition's title, "Museums Are Graveyards," was deliberately ______. Its curators wanted visitors to arrive ready to argue about what museums are for, and judging by the comment cards, they succeeded.
questions.explanation: A title meant to start arguments is designed to cause a strong reaction.

distractors.why: Placid means calm, which would not start arguments.
Prosaic means dull and ordinary, which this bold title is not.
Inept means clumsy or unskilled, but the title worked as intended.

definition: needing a great deal of effort and endurance

examples.text: The arduous journey over the mountains took the settlers four months.
Mapping the genome was an arduous task that took thirteen years.
Moving a piano up three flights of stairs is as arduous as it sounds.

confused.note: Arduous means very difficult; ardent means passionate.

questions.passage: The path to the summit is only six kilometers long, but hikers should not be fooled. The climb is ______, rising twelve hundred meters over loose rock, and most parties need a full day to complete it.
questions.explanation: A steep climb over loose rock that takes all day demands great effort.

distractors.why: Trivial means of little difficulty or importance, the opposite of this climb.
Tentative means hesitant, which does not describe a trail.
Latent means hidden and undeveloped, which does not fit.

definition: lacking skill or ability

examples.text: The inept commander marched his army into a swamp.
The comedy follows an inept burglar who locks himself inside the bank.
I am so inept at wrapping gifts that mine look like they survived a storm.

confused.note: Inept means lacking skill; inapt means not suitable for the occasion.

questions.passage: The first attempt to restore the fresco was shockingly ______. The restorer used the wrong solvent, dissolved part of the original paint, and then tried to hide the damage with colors that did not match.
questions.explanation: Using the wrong solvent and mismatched colors shows a lack of skill.

distractors.why: Adept means highly skilled, the opposite of this restorer.
Astute means shrewd and perceptive, which this work was not.
Wary means cautious; a cautious restorer would not have dissolved the paint.

definition: quick to notice and understand things, and to use them to one's advantage

examples.text: An astute observer of court politics, she knew which ministers were about to fall.
An astute technician noticed that the samples had been stored at the wrong temperature.
My astute little sister figured out where the gifts were hidden within an hour.

confused.note: Astute describes a clever, perceptive mind; acute means sharp or severe, as in "acute pain."

questions.passage: Few buyers saw any value in the abandoned warehouse district. One ______ investor, noticing that artists had begun renting studios there, bought six buildings, and within a decade they were worth twenty times what she had paid.
questions.explanation: Spotting an early sign of change and profiting from it shows shrewd perception.

distractors.why: Inept means unskilled, the opposite of this investor.
Haughty means arrogant, which is not what the passage shows.
Prosaic means dull and unimaginative, but she saw what others missed.

definition: shockingly obvious, said of something wrong or bad

examples.text: The seizure of the ship was a flagrant violation of the treaty.
The mayor's flagrant lies fool no one in the village.
Parking across two spaces is a flagrant breach of parking lot manners.

confused.note: Flagrant means glaringly wrong; fragrant means sweet-smelling.

questions.passage: The player's foul was not a matter of interpretation. It was a ______ violation, committed directly in front of the referee and shown on the stadium's giant screen while forty thousand fans watched.
questions.explanation: A foul committed openly in front of everyone is glaringly obvious.

distractors.why: Latent means hidden, the opposite of a foul everyone saw.
Tentative means hesitant or provisional, which does not describe an obvious foul.
Fragrant means sweet-smelling; it only looks like the right word.

definition: proud in a way that shows contempt for others

examples.text: The haughty duchess will not speak to anyone below the rank of earl.
The conqueror's haughty reply to the peace offer was a single word.
The haughty waiter looked at my sneakers as if they had insulted him.

confused.note: Haughty means arrogant; hearty means warm and vigorous.

questions.passage: The famous conductor was admired for his talent and disliked for his manner. He was ______ with younger musicians, refusing to learn their names and addressing them only as "second violin" or "you in the back."
questions.explanation: Refusing to learn names shows proud contempt for others.

distractors.why: Amicable means friendly, the opposite of his manner.
Wary means cautious, which is not what the passage describes.
Stoic means enduring hardship calmly, which does not fit rudeness.

definition: designed to impress others by showing off wealth or importance

examples.text: The banker's ostentatious mansion had a ballroom for every season.
She dislikes ostentatious jewelry and wears only her mother's plain ring.
A gold-plated phone case seems a bit ostentatious.

confused.note: Ostentatious means showy; ostensible means appearing to be true but perhaps not.

questions.passage: The senator preferred to give quietly, and she disapproved of ______ charity. She once declined to attend a fundraising dinner because donors' names were to be projected on the wall in letters three feet high.
questions.explanation: Names projected in giant letters make giving a showy display.

distractors.why: Furtive means secretive, the opposite of names on a wall.
Prudent means wise and careful, which she would not disapprove of.
Elusive means hard to find or catch, which does not describe showy giving.

definition: ordinary and lacking imagination or excitement

examples.text: After the poetry of the first chapter, the prosaic second chapter disappoints.
The mysterious lights had a prosaic explanation: headlights on a distant road.
My summer was prosaic: work, sleep, and laundry.

confused.note: Prosaic means dull and ordinary; a mosaic is a picture made of small tiles.

questions.passage: Rumors spread that the sealed room in the old library held forbidden manuscripts. When it was finally opened, its contents proved disappointingly ______: stacks of water bills and a broken typewriter.
questions.explanation: Water bills and a broken typewriter are ordinary and unexciting.

distractors.why: Provocative means stirring up strong reactions, which old bills do not.
Ignominious means shameful, which does not describe water bills.
Replete means filled with something and needs "with"; it cannot stand alone here.

definition: to give a false idea of something, or to show that something is not true

examples.text: Her calm voice belies the fear that the reader knows she feels.
The lake's still surface belies the strong currents beneath it.
His messy desk belies how organized he actually is.

confused.note: To belie is to give a false impression of something; to betray a feeling is to reveal it unintentionally.

questions.passage: The building's plain brick exterior ______ what lies within. Visitors who step through its unmarked door find a soaring hall of colored glass and one of the finest collections of modern sculpture in the country.
questions.explanation: The plain outside gives a false impression of the grand interior.

distractors.why: Confirms means shows to be true, but the outside misleads.
Curtails means cuts short, which does not fit.
Espouses means supports a cause, which a building cannot do.

definition: to make a law, rule, or idea widely known, especially officially

examples.text: The emperor promulgated a new code of laws in every province.
The agency promulgated stricter rules for testing drinking water.
The coach promulgated a team rule: no phones in the locker room.

confused.note: Promulgate means to announce a law or idea officially; propagate means to spread or to breed.

questions.passage: Writing a new safety code was only half the task. The ministry also had to ______ it, printing copies for every factory and sending inspectors to explain the changes to owners who might never read an official gazette.
questions.explanation: Printing copies and sending inspectors makes the code widely and officially known.

distractors.why: Rescind means to cancel officially, the opposite of publicizing a new code.
Belie means to give a false impression of, which does not fit.
Deter means to discourage, which is not what the ministry does to its own code.

definition: unusual and slightly strange in behavior or style

examples.text: The eccentric inventor wore a different colored hat for each day of the week.
An eccentric aunt who keeps owls in the attic is the novel's most memorable character.
Our eccentric neighbor mows his lawn at midnight wearing a headlamp.

confused.note: Eccentric means odd in a harmless, individual way; erratic means unpredictable and unsteady.

questions.passage: The mathematician's habits were ______ but harmless. He ate the same lunch for thirty years, refused to use any pen that was not green, and worked only while standing on one particular floorboard.
questions.explanation: Green pens and a favorite floorboard are odd, individual habits.

distractors.why: Conventional means ordinary and expected, which these habits are not.
Haughty means arrogant, which the passage does not suggest.
Flagrant means shockingly wrong, far too strong for harmless quirks.

definition: friendly and without serious disagreement

examples.text: The two colonies reached an amicable settlement of their border dispute.
The partners part on amicable terms, each wishing the other well.
The trade of my sandwich for her chips was entirely amicable.

confused.note: Amicable describes relationships and agreements; amiable describes a friendly person.

questions.passage: Observers expected the division of the company to end in court. To their surprise the process was ______: the founders met over coffee, split the assets in an afternoon, and remained friends afterward.
questions.explanation: Settling over coffee and staying friends shows a friendly process without serious dispute.

distractors.why: Acrimonious means bitter and angry, which observers expected but did not see.
Arduous means very difficult, but the split took one afternoon.
Ostentatious means showy, which is not the point.

definition: filled or well supplied with something

examples.text: The novel is replete with references to Greek myth.
The harbor was replete with ships from every trading nation.
The attic is replete with boxes nobody has opened in years.

confused.note: Replete means filled with something; complete means whole or finished.

questions.passage: The explorer's journal is ______ with errors. She confuses the names of rivers, records mountains that do not exist, and places one coastal town three hundred miles inland.
questions.explanation: Many mistakes of several kinds show the journal is full of errors.

distractors.why: Devoid means completely lacking, the opposite of a journal full of errors.
Wary means cautious; a journal cannot be cautious with errors.
Stoic means enduring without complaint, which does not fit.

definition: causing public shame or disgrace

examples.text: The invasion ended in an ignominious retreat through the snow.
The villain meets an ignominious end, tripped by a child's toy.
My brief career as goalie came to an ignominious close after the seventh goal.

confused.note: Ignominious means shameful; ignorant means lacking knowledge.

questions.passage: The champion had boasted that the match would be over in minutes. It was, though not as he had planned: his ______ defeat by an unknown teenager was replayed on sports channels for a week.
questions.explanation: Losing quickly to an unknown after boasting is publicly humiliating.

distractors.why: Auspicious means promising success, which a defeat is not.
Amicable means friendly, which does not describe a humiliating loss.
Tentative means hesitant, which does not fit a swift, public defeat.

partsNote: from Latin nomen, "name": without a good name

definition: done on purpose; or slow and careful

examples.text: The delay was deliberate: the general wanted the enemy to run out of food.
The surgeon worked with slow, deliberate movements, checking each stitch before the next.
Leaving the last cookie was a deliberate act of kindness.

confused.note: Deliberate means intentional or careful; deliberative describes a group or process devoted to careful discussion.

questions.passage: The gaps in the composer's score are not mistakes. They are ______ silences, placed so that listeners will notice the sounds of the concert hall itself: a cough, a creaking seat, rain on the roof.
questions.explanation: Silences placed for a purpose are intentional.

distractors.why: Inadvertent means accidental, which the first sentence rules out.
Incessant means never stopping, which cannot describe gaps.
Ignominious means shameful, which is not suggested.

definition: careful because you think there may be danger or a problem

examples.text: Deer are wary animals that bolt at the snap of a twig.
After two broken treaties, the chiefs were wary of a third.
I am wary of any email that begins "Congratulations, winner!"

confused.note: Wary means cautious; weary means tired.

questions.passage: Having lost money on two earlier inventions that never worked, the investors were ______ of the engineer's latest proposal. They asked to see a working model before committing a single dollar.
questions.explanation: Demanding a working model after past losses shows caution.

distractors.why: Weary means tired; it looks like the right word but does not mean cautious.
Credulous means too ready to believe, the opposite of their cautious attitude.
Replete means filled with, which does not fit.

definition: hard to find, catch, achieve, or remember

examples.text: The elusive snow leopard is rarely photographed in the wild.
The right word for the feeling remains elusive to the narrator.
A full night of sleep was elusive the week before finals.

confused.note: Elusive means hard to catch; illusive, a rare word, means based on illusion. Allusive means full of indirect references.

questions.passage: Physicists searched for the particle for nearly fifty years. It proved so ______ that several teams announced its discovery only to withdraw the claim when the signal vanished on closer inspection.
questions.explanation: A particle that kept slipping away from detection is hard to find.

distractors.why: Ubiquitous means found everywhere, the opposite of something so hard to detect.
Prosaic means dull and ordinary, which does not explain a fifty-year search.
Provocative means stirring up reactions, which is not the point.

definition: careful and sensible, especially in avoiding risks

examples.text: The prudent governor stored grain in good years against the bad ones.
It is prudent to repeat an experiment before announcing a surprising result.
It seemed prudent to bring an umbrella, given the color of the sky.

confused.note: Prudent means sensible; prudish means too easily shocked.

questions.passage: With the storm still two days away, some residents thought the mayor's order to stock sandbags was excessive. It proved ______: the river rose a meter higher than forecast, and the sandbags saved the town's lower streets.
questions.explanation: Preparing early for a flood that came was sensible and careful.

distractors.why: Rash means hasty and careless, but the order was wise foresight.
Ostentatious means showy, which is not the issue.
Ignominious means shameful, which a successful precaution is not.

definition: existing but not yet active, developed, or visible

examples.text: The virus can remain latent in nerve cells for decades.
The quiet clerk's latent courage appears only when the village floods.
The art class brought out a latent talent for drawing I never knew I had.

confused.note: Latent means hidden or undeveloped; patent, as an adjective, means obvious.

questions.passage: The seeds had lain in the desert soil for years, showing no sign of life. Their ______ ability to sprout was revealed only when an unusually heavy rain soaked the ground and the valley turned green within a week.
questions.explanation: An ability that exists but stays hidden until rain comes is undeveloped and unseen.

distractors.why: Flagrant means glaringly obvious, the opposite of something showing no sign.
Eccentric means odd, which does not describe a hidden ability.
Deliberate means intentional, which seeds cannot be.

definition: enduring pain or hardship without showing feelings or complaining

examples.text: The stoic soldiers marched for days on half rations without complaint.
The stoic farmer buries his grief in work.
My sister was stoic at the dentist and did not flinch once.

confused.note: Stoic means bearing hardship without complaint; stolid means showing little emotion or interest at all.

questions.passage: The marathon runner fell at the thirtieth kilometer and finished with a badly scraped knee. She was ______ about it, waving away the medics and telling reporters only that the last stretch had been "a bit uncomfortable."
questions.explanation: Downplaying an injury and refusing help shows endurance without complaint.

distractors.why: Petulant means sulky and childish, the opposite of her calm.
Haughty means arrogant, which is not what her modest remark shows.
Tentative means hesitant, which does not fit.

partsNote: from the Stoa, the porch in Athens where Stoic philosophers taught

definition: very brave and not afraid of danger

examples.text: The intrepid pilot crossed the Atlantic alone in an open cockpit.
An intrepid team of divers mapped the flooded cave system.
Our intrepid dog marched straight up to the vacuum cleaner and barked at it.

confused.note: Intrepid means without fear; trepidation means fear or anxiety.

questions.passage: The reporter was nothing if not ______. To document conditions in the flooded region, she paddled alone for three days through waters full of debris, sleeping on rooftops along the way.
questions.explanation: Paddling alone through dangerous floodwater shows fearless bravery.

distractors.why: Timid means easily frightened, the opposite of her conduct.
Wary means cautious; someone this cautious would not have gone alone.
Prosaic means dull and ordinary, which this journey was not.

definition: continuing without stopping, in an annoying way

examples.text: The incessant pounding of waves has carved caves into the cliff.
The narrator cannot think for the incessant ticking of the hall clock.
The incessant beeping of the smoke detector kept us up all night.

confused.note: Incessant means never stopping; incisive means sharp and clear.

questions.passage: Residents near the new airport complained less about the loudness of the planes than about how ______ the noise was. From five in the morning until midnight there was scarcely a minute without an engine overhead.
questions.explanation: Noise with scarcely a minute's break continues without stopping.

distractors.why: Sporadic means occasional, the opposite of nonstop noise.
Latent means hidden, which loud engines are not.
Amicable means friendly, which does not describe noise.

definition: having mixed or opposing feelings about something

examples.text: The narrator is ambivalent about returning home, both longing for it and dreading it.
Many colonists were ambivalent about independence until the fighting began.
I am ambivalent about the new schedule: later start, but later finish.

confused.note: Ambivalent describes a person's mixed feelings; ambiguous describes words or situations that are unclear.

questions.passage: The town's residents are ______ about the proposed factory. They welcome the eight hundred jobs it would bring, yet they fear what its smokestacks would do to the valley's air.
questions.explanation: Welcoming the jobs while fearing the pollution is having mixed feelings.

distractors.why: Ambiguous describes unclear words or situations, not people with mixed feelings.
Indifferent means not caring either way, but residents care strongly in both directions.
Intrepid means fearless, yet the residents have fears.

definition: calm and not easily upset or disturbed

examples.text: The placid lake reflected the mountains like a mirror.
Her placid expression gives no hint of the storm inside.
Our placid old horse did not even blink when the fireworks started.

confused.note: Placid is an adjective meaning calm; placate is a verb meaning to calm someone.

questions.passage: Kayakers who had braced for rough water found the bay unexpectedly ______. There was no wind, the surface was as smooth as glass, and the only ripples came from their own paddles.
questions.explanation: Smooth, windless water is calm and undisturbed.

distractors.why: Turbulent means rough and stormy, which is what they had braced for.
Elusive means hard to find, which does not describe calm water.
Incessant means never stopping, which does not fit.

definition: not friendly or willing to take part; distant

examples.text: The aloof heir watches the dancing from a corner and speaks to no one.
The republic stayed aloof from the quarrels of its larger neighbors.
The cat remains aloof until someone opens a can of tuna.

confused.note: Aloof means emotionally distant; aloft means up in the air.

questions.passage: New students often mistook the professor's shyness for coldness. Because she rarely smiled and never lingered after class, she seemed ______, though those who visited her office found her generous with her time.
questions.explanation: Rarely smiling and never lingering make her seem distant.

distractors.why: Garrulous means very talkative, which she was not.
Impetuous means rash and impulsive, which does not fit a reserved person.
Frugal means careful with money, which is unrelated.

definition: to reduce or limit something

examples.text: Wartime rationing curtailed the use of sugar and gasoline.
The drought forced farmers to curtail irrigation by half.
I curtailed my screen time after noticing I had spent six hours on my phone.

confused.note: Curtail means to cut short; it has no connection to a curtain.

questions.passage: The festival normally runs for ten days. This year, because two of its main venues were damaged by flooding, organizers had to ______ the program to a single weekend.
questions.explanation: Cutting ten days to one weekend reduces the program.

distractors.why: Prolong means to make longer, the opposite of what happened.
Venerate means to regard with deep respect, which does not fit.
Espouse means to support a cause, which is not what organizers did to the program.

definition: harshly critical or sarcastic; or able to burn by chemical action

examples.text: The reviewer's caustic wit made authors dread her column.
Caustic soda will burn skin on contact and must be handled with gloves.
His caustic comment about my cooking stung more than he intended.

confused.note: Caustic means biting or burning; acoustic relates to sound.

questions.passage: The columnist was feared for her ______ reviews. Of one new restaurant she wrote that the soup "tasted of regret" and that the only thing warm about the place was the bill.
questions.explanation: Witty, cutting insults are harshly critical.

distractors.why: Insipid means bland and lacking flavor, the opposite of her sharp writing.
Wistful means sadly longing, which does not describe insults.
Didactic means intended to teach, which is not the tone of these jabs.

definition: a person with outstanding skill, especially in music or another art

examples.text: Paganini was the most celebrated violin virtuoso of his century.
The novel's heroine is a chess virtuoso who has never lost a tournament.
My grandmother is a virtuoso of the grill, and her ribs draw the whole block.

confused.note: A virtuoso is a brilliant performer; virtuous means morally good.

questions.passage: By the age of twelve the pianist was already a ______. She could play the most demanding concertos from memory, and audiences across Europe filled halls to hear her.
questions.explanation: Playing the hardest works from memory shows outstanding skill.

distractors.why: A novice is a beginner, the opposite of this performer.
An iconoclast attacks accepted beliefs, which is not described.
A partisan is a strong supporter of one side, which does not fit.

definition: not relevant or not belonging to the matter at hand

examples.text: Researchers filtered out extraneous noise from the recording.
The editor removed extraneous subplots so the main story could breathe.
Leave out the extraneous details and just tell me who won.

confused.note: Extraneous means beside the point; extensive means large in amount or area.

questions.passage: The first version of the survey asked respondents about their favorite colors, pets, and hobbies before reaching the questions on commuting. Designers cut this ______ material, and completion rates rose sharply.
questions.explanation: Questions about pets and hobbies do not belong in a commuting survey.

distractors.why: Pertinent means relevant, which this material was not.
Detrimental means harmful; the material is described as beside the point.
Hackneyed means overused, which does not describe unrelated questions.

definition: intended to teach, sometimes in a preachy way

examples.text: The fable's didactic ending spells out its moral in capital letters.
Medieval plays were often didactic, staging lessons about virtue and vice.
My uncle's stories always turn didactic around the ten-minute mark.

confused.note: Didactic means meant to teach; dialectic is reasoning through the exchange of opposing arguments.

questions.passage: Children's books of the 1800s were openly ______. Almost every story ended with a lazy boy punished or a truthful girl rewarded, and many closed with a rhyme stating the lesson in case any reader had missed it.
questions.explanation: Stories built around a stated lesson are meant to teach.

distractors.why: Whimsical means playful and fanciful, the opposite of these moral lessons.
Caustic means harshly sarcastic, which these stories are not.
Impeccable means flawless, which is not the point.

definition: to adopt or support a belief, cause, or way of life

examples.text: The young duke espoused the cause of the peasants, to his family's horror.
Few biologists now espouse the theory that the trait is purely inherited.
My roommate espouses a strict "no shoes indoors" philosophy.

confused.note: Espouse means to support a cause; expose means to uncover.

questions.passage: In her youth the economist ______ the view that markets should be left entirely alone. After studying several financial crises, she abandoned that position and began calling for stronger oversight.
questions.explanation: She held and supported a view that she later abandoned.

distractors.why: Curtailed means cut short; one supports or rejects a view, one does not shorten it.
Deterred means discouraged someone from acting, which does not fit a view.
Venerated means revered almost as sacred, too strong for holding an economic opinion.

definition: based on a mistaken belief or faulty reasoning

examples.text: The claim rests on the fallacious assumption that correlation proves cause.
The fallacious belief that the city could not be taken left its walls unguarded.
It is fallacious to think that the most expensive phone must be the best.

confused.note: Fallacious describes a mistaken argument; fallible describes a person who can make mistakes.

questions.passage: The advertisement argues that because most champions wear the brand's shoes, the shoes must make runners faster. This reasoning is ______: the company simply pays the fastest runners to wear its products.
questions.explanation: The argument mistakes a paid arrangement for cause and effect, so its reasoning is faulty.

distractors.why: Impeccable means flawless, the opposite of this argument.
Extraneous means irrelevant; the reasoning is on topic but wrong.
Morose means gloomy, which does not describe reasoning.

definition: lacking flavor, interest, or energy

examples.text: Critics called the sequel insipid, a pale copy of the original.
Distilled water tastes insipid because it contains no dissolved minerals.
The cafeteria's insipid soup needed salt, pepper, and possibly a miracle.

confused.note: Insipid means bland; insidious means harmful in a gradual, hidden way.

questions.passage: The chef's early dishes were criticized as ______. Diners complained that the sauces had no seasoning and that every plate, whatever its ingredients, somehow tasted like boiled rice.
questions.explanation: Food with no seasoning that all tastes the same is bland.

distractors.why: Caustic means burning or biting, the opposite of flavorless.
Pungent means sharply strong in taste or smell, which this food was not.
Obdurate means stubborn, which does not describe food.

definition: acting quickly and without thinking about the results

examples.text: The impetuous prince charged before his archers were in position.
Her impetuous decision to board the ship changes the course of the novel.
In an impetuous moment I dyed my hair green the night before picture day.

confused.note: Impetuous means rash; imperious means bossy and commanding.

questions.passage: The company's founder was brilliant but ______. She once bought a rival firm after a single phone call, without asking her accountants to review its books, and spent the next two years paying off its hidden debts.
questions.explanation: Buying a company after one call, with no review, is acting rashly.

distractors.why: Prudent means careful and sensible, which this purchase was not.
Aloof means distant, which is not what the passage describes.
Frugal means careful with money, the opposite of an unexamined purchase.

definition: extreme greed for money or possessions

examples.text: The miser's avarice costs him the love of his only daughter.
The governor's avarice drained the province's treasury within a year.
Avarice got the better of me, and I took the last three slices.

confused.note: Avarice is the noun; avaricious is the adjective meaning greedy.

questions.passage: The folktale is a warning against ______. Its merchant, already the richest man in the city, cheats a widow out of her last coin and is turned to stone with his hand still closed around it.
questions.explanation: A rich man cheating a widow for one more coin shows extreme greed.

distractors.why: Altruism means selfless concern for others, the opposite of the merchant's conduct.
Cacophony means harsh noise, which is unrelated.
Candor means honesty, which is not what the tale warns against.

definition: unhappy, gloomy, and unwilling to talk

examples.text: The morose gatekeeper answers every greeting with a grunt.
After the defeat, the once cheerful general grew morose and withdrew from court.
My brother was morose for a week after his team lost the final.

confused.note: Morose means gloomy and sullen; morbid means having an unhealthy interest in death or disease.

questions.passage: Since the factory closed, the once lively café has taken on a ______ air. Its few remaining customers sit alone, stirring their coffee in silence and staring at the rain.
questions.explanation: Silent customers staring at the rain create a gloomy mood.

distractors.why: Jovial means cheerful and friendly, which describes the café as it used to be.
Impetuous means rash, which does not fit a quiet, sad scene.
Placid means calm and untroubled; the scene is quiet, but its mood is sad, not peaceful.

definition: used so often that it has lost its meaning or effect

examples.text: The script relies on the hackneyed device of long-lost twins.
Even in 1900, critics called the patriotic verses hackneyed.
"Reach for the stars" is a hackneyed yearbook quote.

confused.note: Nearly identical in meaning; hackneyed stresses that a phrase or idea is worn out from long use.

questions.passage: The film's plot, in which a retired detective is drawn back for one last case, is thoroughly ______. Its dialogue, however, is so sharp and surprising that viewers quickly forget how familiar the story is.
questions.explanation: A plot seen many times before is worn out from overuse.

distractors.why: Intricate means complex; the contrast with surprising dialogue calls for a word meaning overly familiar.
Impeccable means flawless, but the plot is being criticized.
Extraneous means irrelevant, but the plot is the film's main story.

definition: to feel or show deep respect for someone or something

examples.text: The townspeople venerated the founder and carved her likeness above every gate.
The young monks venerate the old teacher and copy even his handwriting.
My grandfather venerates his first car and still polishes it every Sunday.

confused.note: Venerate means to revere; generate means to produce.

questions.passage: In her home country the poet is ______. Schoolchildren memorize her verses, her face appears on a banknote, and her birthday is a national holiday.
questions.explanation: Memorized verses, a banknote, and a holiday show deep respect.

distractors.why: Vilified means spoken of as evil, the opposite of such honors.
Curtailed means cut short, which does not apply to a poet.
Deterred means discouraged, which does not fit.

definition: talking a lot, especially about unimportant things

examples.text: The garrulous innkeeper tells each guest the full history of every chair.
The garrulous ambassador accidentally revealed his king's plans at dinner.
A garrulous stranger on the train told me about all nine of his cats.

confused.note: Garrulous means talkative; querulous means complaining.

questions.passage: Passengers who wanted a quiet ride learned to avoid the ______ driver of the number nine bus. Between any two stops he could describe his nephew's wedding, his opinion of the mayor, and the weather forecast for the next ten days.
questions.explanation: Chatting at length about trivial topics is being excessively talkative.

distractors.why: Taciturn means saying very little, the opposite of this driver.
Morose means gloomy and unwilling to talk, which he was not.
Adamant means firmly insistent, which is not the trait described.

definition: stubbornly refusing to change one's mind or feelings

examples.text: The obdurate king ignored every petition for mercy.
Her father remains obdurate, and the lovers must meet in secret.
My little brother was obdurate about not wearing a coat, even in the snow.

confused.note: Obdurate means stubborn; obsolete means out of date.

questions.passage: Neighbors, engineers, and finally the mayor herself urged the landowner to sell the narrow strip the new bridge required. He remained ______, refusing every offer and insisting he would never part with a single meter.
questions.explanation: Refusing every appeal and offer is stubbornly unyielding.

distractors.why: Amenable means willing to agree, which he was not.
Indifferent means not caring, but he cared intensely about keeping the land.
Wistful means sadly longing, which does not describe his refusal.

definition: to keep changing between different opinions or choices

examples.text: The king vacillated between war and peace until the enemy decided for him.
Hamlet vacillates for most of the play before he acts.
I vacillated between the two colleges until the day before the deadline.

confused.note: People vacillate between choices; objects oscillate, swinging regularly back and forth.

questions.passage: The committee could not make up its mind. For months it ______ between renovating the old library and building a new one, voting first for one plan and then, at the next meeting, for the other.
questions.explanation: Voting for one plan and then the other is wavering between choices.

distractors.why: Persevered means kept steadily to a course, which the committee did not.
Espoused means supported a cause; the committee could not settle on which plan to support.
Venerated means revered, which does not fit.

definition: refusing to be persuaded or to change one's mind

examples.text: The captain was adamant that the ship would not sail in such weather.
She is adamant in her refusal, and no letter from her family can move her.
Mom was adamant that homework came before video games.

confused.note: Adamant means firm and unpersuadable; obdurate is harsher and suggests hard-hearted stubbornness.

questions.passage: Although several board members urged delay, the director was ______ that the report be published on schedule. She would accept no postponement, she said, even if it meant printing the copies herself.
questions.explanation: Accepting no postponement shows she could not be persuaded.

distractors.why: Ambivalent means having mixed feelings, but she was certain.
Indifferent means not caring, the opposite of her insistence.
Wistful means sadly longing, which does not fit her firmness.

definition: careful to spend little money or use few resources

examples.text: Frugal habits learned in the lean years stayed with her long after she grew rich.
The frugal design uses a third of the energy of earlier models.
Being frugal, I bring lunch from home and save the money for a trip.

confused.note: Frugal is praise for careful spending; miserly is criticism of someone too unwilling to spend.

questions.passage: Despite earning a large salary, the engineer lived in a notably ______ manner. He drove the same car for twenty years, repaired his own shoes, and planted a vegetable garden to cut his grocery bills.
questions.explanation: Keeping an old car, mending shoes, and growing food save money.

distractors.why: Opulent means luxurious, the opposite of his habits.
Impetuous means rash, which these careful habits are not.
Garrulous means talkative, which is unrelated.

definition: feeling a gentle sadness and longing for something past or out of reach

examples.text: The narrator gives a wistful account of summers at her grandmother's farm.
Exiled officers wrote wistful letters about the cafés of the capital.
My dad gets wistful whenever he hears songs from his college years.

confused.note: Wistful means sadly longing; wishful, as in "wishful thinking," means hoping for something unlikely.

questions.passage: The retired ballerina watched the young dancers rehearse with a ______ smile. She was glad for them, she said, yet she could not help remembering the stage lights and wishing she could feel them once more.
questions.explanation: Gladness mixed with longing for her past is gentle, sad yearning.

distractors.why: Caustic means harshly sarcastic, which contradicts being glad for them.
Morose means sullen and gloomy, too dark for someone who is smiling and glad.
Indifferent means not caring, but she clearly feels a great deal.

definition: a harsh, unpleasant mixture of loud sounds

examples.text: The city greets the country boy with a cacophony of horns, bells, and shouting.
At dawn the rainforest erupts in a cacophony of bird and monkey calls.
Band practice on the first day was pure cacophony.

confused.note: Cacophony is harsh noise; euphony is pleasing sound.

questions.passage: Anyone who has stood near an orchestra before a concert knows the ______ of tuning: forty instruments sounding different notes at once, with no rhythm or melody to connect them.
questions.explanation: Forty instruments playing unrelated notes produce harsh, jumbled noise.

distractors.why: Accord means agreement or harmony, the opposite of this clash of sounds.
Avarice means greed, which has nothing to do with sound.
Brevity means shortness, which does not describe noise.

definition: causing harm or damage

examples.text: Lack of sleep is detrimental to memory and attention.
The blockade was detrimental to both countries' merchants.
Skipping breakfast turned out to be detrimental to my morning mood.

confused.note: Detrimental means harmful; determinate means having fixed limits.

questions.passage: The dam brought electricity to thousands of homes, but its effect on the river's fish was ______. Blocked from their spawning grounds upstream, several species declined by more than ninety percent.
questions.explanation: A decline of over ninety percent shows the dam harmed the fish.

distractors.why: Beneficial means helpful, the opposite of the dam's effect on fish.
Impeccable means flawless, which a harmful effect is not.
Didactic means intended to teach, which does not fit.

partsNote: from Latin terere, "to rub": wearing away

definition: to discourage someone from doing something, often through fear or doubt

examples.text: Bright warning colors deter predators from eating the poisonous frog.
High walls did not deter the invaders, who simply dug beneath them.
The long line did not deter us from getting ice cream.

confused.note: Deter means to discourage; defer means to postpone or to yield.

questions.passage: Park officials posted signs describing recent bear sightings on the northern trail. The warnings were meant to ______ hikers from camping there overnight, and for the most part they worked.
questions.explanation: Warnings about bears discourage people from camping.

distractors.why: Entice means to attract, the opposite of what a bear warning does.
Vacillate means to waver, and it cannot take "hikers" as an object.
Venerate means to revere, which does not fit.

definition: having no interest in or concern about something

examples.text: The indifferent sea closes over the wreck without a trace.
Many citizens were indifferent to a war fought so far from home.
My cat is indifferent to the expensive toy and obsessed with the box.

confused.note: Indifferent means not caring; it does not mean "not different."

questions.passage: The critic was neither pleased nor annoyed by the play. She was simply ______ to it, and her review, two short paragraphs on an inside page, suggested that she had forgotten most of it by the time she reached home.
questions.explanation: Being neither pleased nor annoyed and forgetting it quickly shows a lack of interest.

distractors.why: Adamant means firmly insistent, which contradicts having no strong reaction.
Detrimental means harmful, which does not describe a critic's reaction.
Susceptible means easily affected, the opposite of being unmoved.

definition: without any faults or mistakes

examples.text: The forger's work was impeccable, and it fooled experts for fifty years.
The butler's manners are impeccable, which makes his crime harder to believe.
Her timing was impeccable: she walked in just as the pizza arrived.

confused.note: Impeccable means flawless; implacable means impossible to calm or satisfy.

questions.passage: The translation is ______. Reviewers fluent in both languages searched its four hundred pages for a single error of meaning or tone and reported that they could not find one.
questions.explanation: A long work in which no error can be found is flawless.

distractors.why: Fallacious means based on error, the opposite of a flawless translation.
Insipid means bland; the reviewers were checking for errors, and found none.
Hackneyed means overused, which is not what reviewers were testing.
